cards.title: Branded Search & Shopping Campaigns: Structure, Bidding & Exclusions
cards.summary: Build a manual-CPC branded shopping campaign plus branded search to protect your brand term, harvest cheap conversions and keep prospecting bids clean.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing paid search structure for a store that already gets branded searches and wants brand protection plus cheaper conversion data.
steps: Create a separate shopping campaign for branded traffic only (New campaign > Sales > conversion goal Purchases > Shopping > connect Merchant Center > choose Standard shopping, not Performance Max). Name it by brand + campaign type.

Set bidding to manual CPC with a low budget (the source uses ~$50/day) and high campaign priority. Turn off the search network; set locations to where you actually sell and set location options to 'Presence' only, never 'Presence or interest'.

Create a product group/ad group (e.g. all products in one group if the brand term applies to the whole catalog) with a ~$1 starting bid, then subdivide by product only when products differ enough that you want to see separate average CPCs.

Automatically exclude all non-branded terms via a Google Ads script (Tools > Bulk actions > Scripts) so only brand terms remain in the shopping listing. Verify the current script UI before copying anything.
Optionally run a parallel branded search campaign so a branded query shows both shopping and search ads, taking more of the above-the-fold SERP.

In the branded campaign, exclude your existing-customer list: export the customer list from your store backend, then Google Ads > Audiences > Exclusions > upload and exclude. Rationale: repeat buyers searching your name are buying, not browsing, so paying for that click is waste.
Optimize only via manual bids — do not switch to automated bidding; if search impression share is low, raise the max bid slightly instead.

Check whether you are paying for conversions that would have happened organically: the presenter states you usually are, and argues it is still worth it for brand protection, cheap conversion data feeding prospecting, and conversion data that Google uses to steer smart bidding.
Do not expect the campaign to stay clean on its own — continuously exclude non-branded terms and keep the Merchant Center feed optimized, since feed quality drives cost, visibility and click share.
caveats: Source is a Google Ads agency owner with a commercial interest; his 'you always need one' position is his opinion, not a measured benchmark.
Data showed competitors ranking on brand terms; the presenter notes this is mainly seen in software but applies to ecommerce too.
Branded campaigns mostly capture demand that already exists; treat them as protection and data harvesting, not incremental growth.
Automated keyword-removal scripts require account-specific edits and may change — verify the current script interface.

cards.title: Cold Search Campaigns: Capture Problem-Aware Demand, Not Product-Aware Demand
cards.summary: Use broad-match cold search ads on problem-aware queries to reach people who don't know your brand, then tighten winners into exact match.
cards.use_when: Planning acquisition for a store whose product solves a specific problem and whose product-aware search demand is exhausted or too expensive.
steps: Set up a search campaign on the Google network only, objective Sales, single primary conversion action, campaigns optimized for purchase conversions.

Choose bidding: the source uses Maximize Conversions with the AI Max feature on for cold problem-aware terms. He reserves Maximize Clicks for testing product-market fit with broad investigative terms. Turn brand exclusions on so branded queries stay out of this cold campaign.
Set locations with 'Presence' (not presence or interest) limited to countries you actually ship to; set a daily budget you can hold for at least a few weeks of testing.
Build the ad group from many problem-phrased keywords, mixing exact and broad match; the source explicitly avoids phrase match. Start broad to see the full range of queries the market actually types.
Read the search terms report: mine converting broad queries, then promote proven ones to exact match so Google can optimize around them, and pause/remove terms with clicks but no conversions.

Judge terms on click-through rate, CPC and conversion rate together. In the case study, 'how to lower blood pressure' had a 7.5% CTR at 38p CPC and ~2.3% conversion; 'blood pressure supplements' had a higher conversion rate but also a higher CPC; 'how to reduce high blood pressure' had a ~9% CTR with few conversions.
Once a term proves itself, change the final URL for that keyword so the ad points to a page written for that exact query, rather than the generic default landing page.
Build out the ad with price extensions, structured snippets, callouts, sitelinks and a business logo to occupy more of the SERP.

Use dynamic keyword insertion in the headline so the searcher's own phrase appears in the ad (set a sensible default headline for when no keyword is inserted) and pin it; the source credits this congruence for an 8.32% cold CTR.
caveats: Case-study metrics (8.32% CTR, 3.82% cold conversion rate, ~£3.5k spend, £7.6k reported return) are from one UK supplement account over ~3 weeks and are examples, not benchmarks.
The presenter says Google-reported return figures are unreliable and recommends a third-party attribution tool as source of truth.
Broad match floods in irrelevant queries; it requires ongoing search-term review and negative work.

Send problem-aware cold traffic to an advertorial/educational sales letter, not a product page with a buy box — the source states you cannot present an offer to someone who is only problem-aware and brand-unaware.

cards.title: Build Mini-Funnels Per Search Term for Cold Traffic
cards.summary: Match one landing page and one ad per high-volume problem-aware search phrase to convert cold searchers you already know are looking for.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many landing pages to build for paid search and where to spend page-creation effort on problem-aware traffic.
steps: List the problem-aware phrases in your niche with their monthly search volume (the source cites ~3.6k for 'how to lower blood pressure' as an example). Treat each phrase as a separate mini-funnel.
For each phrase, check the three constraints: can the ad get a strong CTR, what CPC can you tolerate at your COGS, and what conversion rate can the page achieve.

Apply constraint thinking: if CTR is already strong (the source reached ~8%) and CPC is acceptable, the biggest lever is conversion rate, so invest in the page for that phrase rather than rewriting the ad.

Create a landing page congruent with the phrase — e.g. for 'how to lower blood pressure' build an educational article/sales letter that lays out the problem and solutions, then presents your product as the solution. Avoid a generic advertorial when the phrase implies a different intent.
Point the keyword's final URL to that page (not just the default ad URL) so the same campaign can hold several mini-funnels.
Keep phrases you have not built a page for yet running to the default page; add pages only for phrases with real search volume and converting signal.

Expect different CPCs by intent: product-aware phrases ('blood pressure supplements') cost more per click than problem phrases, but the problem phrase can still have a lower cost per conversion because it is more congruent with the page.
Because volume is capped per phrase, treat each page as longevity infrastructure — a page converting at 10% CTR on ~4,000 views a quarter compounds over years of the brand's life.
caveats: Search volume limits reach per phrase; this is a demand-capture play, not a way to create new demand.
The conversion-rate estimates in the source are projections from a 3-week test, not a proof that page changes lift conversion.
Distinguish conversions at the page level (purchase conversion rate) from click-through rate on the ad; improving one does not automatically improve the other.

cards.title: Performance Max: What It Is and Where It Fits in the Google Funnel
cards.summary: Treat Performance Max as a middle-of-funnel catch-all engine fed by signals, not a hands-off campaign that replaces search, shopping or YouTube.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add Performance Max to a store's Google account and what budget share and role to assign it.
steps: Understand the incentive: the source argues Performance Max exists partly to force advertisers into YouTube, Display, Discovery and Gmail inventory that previously could not be monetized from search and shopping alone — so it is built to give Google revenue, but still useful to you.

Position Performance Max as the middle-of-funnel catch-all: it covers auctions and placements your search and shopping campaigns lose, and it retargets cold traffic from Meta, TikTok or organic that landed on the Google network via page-view/product-view signals.
Leave a separate top of funnel (YouTube shorts, in-stream, demand gen, display) and bottom of funnel (branded search, branded shopping, product-aware search and shopping).
Allocate roughly 20–30% of budget to Performance Max as a healthy share — the source's heuristic, not a calculated optimum. Use Performance Max as a core engine, not the entire vehicle.
Feed it strong signals before expecting performance: clean Merchant Center feed, optimized product titles, proper purchase conversion tracking, and high-quality creative assets.
Use it as a remarketing mechanism for cold visitors, but exclude brand terms so it does not claim your branded conversions.
Give it both demand capture and demand generation credit: it can catch existing searches/shopping intent and retarget cold visitors across placements within one campaign.
caveats: The source explicitly warns Performance Max is not set-and-forget; he has audited accounts with 90–100% of budget in 11 Performance Max campaigns.
Performance Max has limited reporting transparency, auto-bidding with no manual CPC control, and reduced placement control unless you add exclusions.
Applies to stores with clean feeds, proper conversion tracking and enough volume to satisfy smart bidding; otherwise the source recommends manual search and shopping first.

cards.title: Qualify Your Store for Performance Max Before Launching
cards.summary: Screen for feed quality, tracking, budget and conversion volume before committing a store to Performance Max.
cards.use_when: Assessing whether a store is ready for Performance Max or should stay on manual search and manual shopping.
steps: Check the feed: is the Merchant Center product feed clean, complete and optimized? A poorly optimized feed disqualifies the store in the source's view.
Check tracking: is there one primary purchase conversion action firing accurately (Google & YouTube app for Shopify or Google tag), with no competing primary actions?
Check volume: can the store generate roughly 30–50 conversions per month, which the source gives as the minimum for smart bidding strategies to learn?
Check budget: does the store have at least $50–$100 per day available; the source treats tiny budgets as a bad fit and recommends manual search and manual shopping instead.
If any check fails, do not force Performance Max. Run manual shopping/search, fix the feed and tracking, then revisit.
When you do launch, accept that Performance Max may only be able to generalize from your conversion data — weak data means weak automation.
caveats: $50–$100/day and 30–50 conversions/month are source-specific readiness heuristics, not universal thresholds.
Being 'on shopping' matters because a store with no shopping presence has no feed signal for Performance Max to work with.

cards.title: Set Up a Performance Max Campaign: Bidding, Locations, Devices, Exclusions
cards.summary: Configure a Performance Max campaign with the right bidding strategy, location targeting, device set and brand exclusions.
cards.use_when: Building a new Performance Max campaign inside a Google Ads account.
steps: New campaign > Sales > optimize for Purchases > Performance Max, connect Merchant Center, name with a clear convention.

Choose bidding: the source almost always uses Maximize Conversion Value with a target ROAS derived from the store's break-even ROAS, computed from COGS, gross margin and unit economics; the alternative is Maximize Conversions with a target CPA. Do not copy another brand's ROAS target — it is meaningless without their margin.

Leave the 'customer acquisition' bidding option off (source preference). Instead pursue new customers through offer, ad congruence and audience signals, and measure new-customer ROAS/CPA in a third-party attribution tool such as Triple Whale or Northbeam.
Set locations to the countries you sell in and the correct language; ignore EU political ads if outside the EU.
Add UTM parameters in campaign URL options (or set them post-publish in your attribution tool) so multi-channel reporting is clean.
Turn off tablets and TV screens (source: tablets never; TVs only for dedicated demand gen) and check device splits — mobile usually converts best; keep computers only if their metrics hold up.
Add brand exclusions; the source notes this is not foolproof.
Import customer lists, in-market audiences, custom-intent audiences based on high-intent keywords, competitor brand names and specific websites as audience signals.
Verify current Google Ads interface and feature names before following these steps, as this setup changes frequently.
caveats: Break-even ROAS/CPA is store-specific; there is no universal 'good' ROAS.
Performance Max only offers automated bidding (Maximize Conversions or Maximize Conversion Value), so you cannot control max CPC.
Brand exclusions in Performance Max are described by the source as incomplete protection; verify with brand queries in reporting.
The source's aversion to the customer-acquisition bidding toggle is an opinion, not a tested rule.

cards.title: Structure Performance Max Around Signal Density, Not Campaign Count
cards.summary: Segment Performance Max by product category and country so signals concentrate in one campaign per audience type.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many Performance Max campaigns a store should run and how to split products and geographies.
steps: Split into separate Performance Max campaigns only where audiences and products are genuinely different (e.g. wallets vs luggage) — the source's rule of thumb is that if a shopper would search these separately, they belong in separate campaigns.
Also split by country or region when advertising in multiple locations; never run two locations in one Performance Max campaign.
Otherwise put everything into one campaign and use multiple asset groups inside it for collections or product types.
Match each asset group's targeting, messaging and audience signals to that specific product segment.
Avoid fragmenting signals across many campaigns and hoping Google optimizes at account level — the source states it does not.
Continually review product performance and remove SKUs that burn budget without converting.
Audit regularly for the failure pattern the source describes: 90–100% of budget concentrated in many Performance Max campaigns with misfired signals, and branded conversions costing $5–$10 per click.
caveats: The 'one campaign per category/country' guidance is a heuristic from the presenter's agency experience, not a controlled benchmark.
Asset-group-level reporting is limited compared to search and shopping, so mis-allocation can hide inside a campaign.

cards.title: Select Products for Performance Max: Scalers, Zombie Asset Groups and 80/20
cards.summary: Choose the products Performance Max focuses on using the 80/20 principle, and quarantine underperformers instead of letting them dilute spend.
cards.use_when: Building or pruning the product list inside a Performance Max campaign.
steps: Apply the Pareto principle: first find the 20% of products generating 80% of revenue, and even the 4% generating 96%; start Performance Max there.
Pick the product that best leads on cold traffic as the primary scaler, i.e. the offer a brand-unaware buyer can be sold on.
Regularly review performance and remove SKUs that consume budget without converting.
For larger catalogs, create 'zombie asset groups' that group only underperforming products, so they can be tested without dragging down the main scaling campaign.
Do not neglect dedicated product pages for those zombie products, and still optimize them — some products simply do not work on Google, and the goal is to keep them from hurting your scalers.
Keep impressions and clicks concentrated on proven high-converting products because every impression and click in Performance Max is a budget decision.
caveats: This is the source's strategy, not a tested attribution model; the 80/20 and 4/96 splits are illustrative distributions.
Removing products from Performance Max does not mean they cannot sell elsewhere (email, organic, other channels).

cards.title: Handle Performance Max's Reporting, Placement and CPC Limitations
cards.summary: Mitigate Performance Max's attribution credit, placement leakage and uncontrolled CPC with third-party measurement, audits and exclusions.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing Performance Max campaign for wasted spend or unreliable reporting.
steps: Use a third-party attribution tool (Triple Whale, Northbeam) as the source of truth because Performance Max can take credit for sales originating in other marketing channels.

Where campaign-level granularity is missing, apply a third-party reporting script (the source names Mike Rhodes'/Microscript as the gold standard) to get placement, cost and conversion detail inside the campaign. Note that Google is rolling out some equivalent transparency, but the source says it is not yet close.
Audit landing pages and placements Performance Max is serving to; if you see irrelevant placements, exclude them and turn off automations you never opted into.
Exclude branded terms inside the Performance Max account so brand conversions are not counted as Performance Max results.
When you cannot control CPC, decide whether the achieved CPC is sustainable at your cost-to-LTV ratio — the source argues that if the economics hold, CPC alone is not the metric to monitor.

Judge launch success weekly: if CPCs remain outside what your margins can sustain even with correct setup, the source's conclusion is that this channel/strategy may simply not be viable for that product and competition level.
Apply the same discipline to unit economics as for other platforms: the platform delivers conversions at a market CPA, and the question is whether your business can hold that CPA.
caveats: Reduced control is inherent to Performance Max bidding; you cannot set a manual max CPC.
Attribution overlap with other channels means platform-reported ROAS is usually optimistic.
Script tools and third-party features change; verify the current interface before implementing.
The 'if CPC is sustainable, don't worry about it' framing is the presenter's economics-based opinion; it still requires monitoring CPA against margin.

cards.title: Audience Signals and Conversion Data Are the Real Performance Max Inputs
cards.summary: Supply customer lists, in-market and custom-intent audiences plus clean conversion tracking so Performance Max can start without a learning plateau.
cards.use_when: Launching a Performance Max campaign from a cold start or improving an underperforming one by changing its inputs.
steps: Verify account-level conversion tracking is accurate before launch: exactly one primary purchase conversion action, tied to your campaign goal, firing via the Google & YouTube app or Google tag.
Upload your customer list and, if allowed, in-market audiences that historically work.
Build custom-intent audiences from high-intent keywords, competitor brand names, specific sites and trigger behaviours relevant to your category.
Include the same audiences as signals even when running feed-only broad campaigns; Performance Max still needs an explicit definition of who your buyer is and is not.
Use exclusions to define who not to reach (existing customers, irrelevant audiences) alongside positive signals.
Expect Performance Max to find the right users eventually, but use strong signals to launch cold from scratch without a long ramp.
caveats: The source still relies on third-party reporting for new-customer measurement rather than the account-level 'customer acquisition' bidding option, which he never enables.
Signal quality depends on available data; a small store may not have enough customer list or conversion volume for full audience-building.

cards.title: Use Search Terms and Landing Page Audits to Fix Google Ads Waste
cards.summary: Regularly review search terms and landing pages to remove non-converting queries and unreviewed placements that drain budget.
cards.use_when: Running weekly/monthly maintenance on Google search, shopping or Performance Max campaigns.
steps: Pull the search terms report and sort by conversions and conversion value.
Remove terms that receive clicks but no conversions, and promote converting broad terms to exact match so budget concentrates on proven queries.
Check whether your best-converting queries are being served by a generic landing page; if so, build a page congruent with that query and change the keyword's final URL.
In Performance Max, audit which landing pages placements are sending traffic to and exclude placements that would never convert.

Remember that the campaign build is only half the job: for shopping campaigns, most ongoing optimization happens in Google Merchant Center, so keep the feed updated or you will see higher cost, lower visibility and reduced click share.
Re-check audience exclusions (especially existing customers) so spend is reserved for net-new demand.
caveats: Search-term data requires statistical significance; a few clicks with no conversions is not conclusive proof that a term should be killed.
For search, keyword-level final URL changes interact with ad-level URLs; verify which URL the system is actually using in the current interface.
